extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, judges, agency attorneys, and advanced students of administrative governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies rule-of-law norms and procedural criteria governing agency lawmaking and notice (publicity, clarity, prospectivity, stability, scope of authority, choice of policymaking form, guidance documents, and decisional allocation) for notice-and-comment and related administrative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisional allocation / personal duty of officeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal authorization (and duty) is relative to officeholders, not an impersonal authorization to government as a whole; delegates must view duties as their own and exercise independent judgment rather than treating direction from superiors as a sufficient legal ground for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The official should be "independently convinced of the action’s legality and appropriateness." "Someone told me to do it" is excluded as a sufficient ground for action. This role-specification spreads accountability through the bureaucracy: all those with delegated authority must exercise their own independent legal judgment. The President must persuade the official rather than issue a direction that substitutes for the delegate’s legal responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultra vires principle / agencies must act within scope of delegated power
rubrics_metrics.description: Because agencies only have powers granted to them by statute, the rule of law requires that an agency act within the scope of that delegated power; only authorized action is valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should review whether the agency has acted within the scope of its authority—the Chevron step-one question. This is a foundational constraint on administrative action (the ultra vires principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent judicial determination of scope with deference to agency (Chevron step-one informed by Skidmore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should independently determine whether Congress has spoken to the precise question (Chevron step one), but that independent judicial judgment may be informed by and give weight to the agency’s views (Skidmore weight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professor Strauss advocates a middle position: the lines defining an agency’s 'Chevron space' must be judicially determined (a statement of what the law is), but that determination should be informed by agency judgments in ways conventional since 1827. Independent review does not exclude giving weight to agency judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skidmore weight factors for agency interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: When affording weight to an agency’s interpretations, courts should consider the thoroughness of the agency’s consideration, validity of its reasoning, consistency with earlier and later pronouncements, and other factors that give the agency power to persuade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skidmore regards agency rulings as representing 'a body of experience and informed judgment' to which courts may resort for guidance; when lacking power to control, persuasiveness depends on those enumerated factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shape of ultra vires review should reflect institutional allocation of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The form and intensity of ultra vires (scope) review should take account of the structure of government and the place of agencies within it, allowing independent judicial review that nonetheless respects agencies’ institutional role and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specification grounds a middle approach: ensure compliance with law by judicial determination while permitting respectful consideration of agency views where appropriate; fidelity to legal allocation of authority requires accommodation of agency expertise when identifying the agency's sphere of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core notice principles for law (publicity, clarity, consistency, prospectivity, stability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law that guides private conduct must meet formal characteristics: publicity, clarity, consistency, prospectivity, and stability; these are central rule-of-law demands for action-guiding legal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law falls short on these dimensions, individuals lack reasonable notice. These principles derive from Fuller and Raz and constitute criteria for evaluating whether agency-made law adequately guides behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice principles apply to agency actions that bind private parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice demands (publicity, clarity, prospectivity, stability, consistency) properly apply to legal sources that bind the public — notably rules and decisions issued by administrative agencies — not merely to delegating statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because regulatory statutes often regulate government behavior rather than private conduct, attention must focus on how agency outputs (rules, guidance, adjudications) embody these formal values; agency development and enunciation of administrative policy provide the specification of what the law demands of private parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking generally preferable to adjudication for notice values
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking tends to better satisfy notice values (prospectivity, clarity, publicity, generality) than case-by-case adjudication, which can create retroactive rules and undesirable variation among individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative adjudication, like common-law processes, often creates rules in the process of application and may apply retroactively to prior facts; where notice values matter, agencies should favor rulemaking unless justified otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to justify choice of policymaking form
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should justify their institutional choice among policymaking forms (rulemaking, adjudication, guidance, etc.), at least by making a comparative assessment explaining why a non-rulemaking form was selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although current doctrine (Chenery II) leaves choice primarily to agencies and no reason-giving requirement is imposed, a modest rule-of-law demand is that agencies provide some justification—e.g., lack of knowledge about statutory impacts or timing concerns—so that agencies self-consciously evaluate forms and bridge internal silos. Such justification could be procedural (similar to the Regulatory Flexibility Act’s analysis) even if not judicially enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to issue prospective guidance when rulemaking impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: When rulemaking is not practicable, agencies have an obligation to issue prospective guidance as a second-best way to satisfy notice principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance documents are agency statements of general applicability and future effect that set forth policy or interpretation without binding force; agencies’ reliance on guidance has prompted criticism and calls for increased scrutiny. Guidance should aim to be prospective and publicly accessible to help guide regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public access to private standards incorporated by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should not rely on private standards that are not practically accessible to the public (e.g., behind paywalls); incorporation by reference raises publicity and access concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars (and Strauss) have forcefully critiqued agency reliance on private standards not practically accessible without a fee and argued for full digital access without charge when private standards are incorporated into rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should develop institutional structures for choosing policymaking forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies as institutions should develop structures and processes to make informed allocations among policymaking forms, rather than leaving that choice to ad hoc organizational dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because organizational factors often drive whether agencies pursue rulemaking or adjudication, establishing mechanisms for comparative assessment and deliberation would improve compliance with rule-of-law notice values; mandatory controls may be impractical, but structural reforms and justification requirements are feasible.
